source_title: How Dropkick Murphys Became Punk’s Loudest Anti-Trump Voice
source_excerpt:
I t’s time to get off the stage, but Ken Casey isn’t done talking to the union electricians yet.
The Dropkick Murphys frontman has been sitting there for 29 minutes and counting, legs dangling off the side of the temporary fixture in the middle of a San Diego street, as he talks with the dwindling crowd on a warm September night. He’s taking selfies, shaking hands, and accepting union challenge coins, small metal disks commemorating the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers’ 41st annual convention, where Dropkicks just performed.
Nine-forty-five. Ten p.m. He keeps going. His bandmates are long gone; members of his management team grumble to each other that they would like to go, too. The techs clear the stage, and Casey barely even turns around as one of them removes a mic from inside his shirt. There he stays, talking to each and every person who wants to tell him how meaningful his band has been to them. “Cool human interactions,” as he later describes them. “Without those people, I wouldn’t be in the position I’m in, you know?”
This is the fourth union convention Dropkick Murphys have played this year. He’d be here after any show, since he likes to talk to his fans. But this audience is special to him. His grandfather, who helped raise him after his father died, was a union organizer in their hometown of Boston , and for most of Casey’s childhood, he figured that would be his path, too. Tonight, even as his energy fades, he doesn’t want a single audience member to feel that he didn’t give them the attention they deserve. Dropkicks are a union band, from a union town, built on union values, and that’s a responsibility Casey takes very seriously.
During their set, Casey, 57, took numerous opportunities to preach to the thousands of electricians who came out. “The truth is that the current president of the United States wouldn’t piss on any of us if we were on fire,” he says, the six other members of his band at attention behind him, his thick Boston accent making him sound like a lost punk-rock Kennedy. “You know it. I know it. But the problem is far worse than even him. It has to do with the wealth gap. It has to do with all these criminals that have taken all the blood, sweat, and tears that we’ve worked for over the years, trying to take away our rights, trying to make it harder for not only us, but for our children and the next generation of people trying to build lives for themselves. Hopefully what comes out of all these horrible times is a much stronger and a much less divided America, and a much less divided working class, and powerful unions. So this one’s for everyone who’s sick of this shit.” Another pause, before he shouts into the mic: “Are you with uuuuus ?” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

They launch into “Who Will Stand With Us?,” the lead single off last year’s For the People . The crowd jumps around, bearded men in the front singing along, kids on their parents’ shoulders pumping fists in the air, catharsis at the end of a long summer. If Woody Guthrie had a taste for slam-dancing in a hardcore pit with bagpipe accompaniment, this song would be his jam.
When Dropkicks formed in 1996, they weren’t known as a particularly political band. Sure, they sang about union life, but they also had a cop-friendly song (“John Law”) and a lot of lyrics about getting fucked up and fighting other kids in Boston. Their politics were of loyalty, pride, and hard work. It didn’t take long for them to become punk-festival headliners, hometown heroes who opened for the Red Sox at Fenway Park, and even a household name after Martin Scorsese used their song “I’m Shipping Up to Boston” in 2006’s The Departed . But these days, they’ve become better known as the band behind a loud, pissed-off, working-class fuck-you aimed squarely at Donald Trump and his cronies. They’ve gone viral for telling off MAGA fans in the audience, and for calling the president “the greatest swindler in the history of the world.” As their songs and music videos get more pointedly focused on their old-school-blue values, they’ve used collaborations with the Guthrie estate, Billy Bragg, and Bruce Springsteen to drive that point home. Casey’s refusal to back down has earned him some powerful friends, like Gov. Maura Healey, the chief executive of his home state. “Ken’s never lost sight of who he is or where he came from,” she tells me, noting that she was a fan long before they met. She named Sept. 25, 2025, Dropkick Murphys Day in Massachusetts, and around the same time, she and her wife, Joanna Lydgate, took Casey, his mom, and his girlfriend as their personal guests to the gala where he was named Massachusetts Storyteller of the Year. “He’s tough, he’s direct, he’s irreverent, he’s loyal, he’s deeply rooted in his community,” Healey adds. “That’s something that a lot of people in Massachusetts really resonate with.”
But it’s not just Massachusetts, or even New England. Across the country, more and more fans are identifying with Casey’s overwhelming frustration with the current state of our democracy. “Eighty percent of America, I think, in their heart of hearts, would say, ‘Man, it’d be good if we could get back to some form of dialogue,’” Casey says. “Sometimes I’m a source of that, and sometimes it’s me flipping off the guy in a MAGA hat in front of the stage. I’m only human — I don’t get it right every time. But it’s better than staying quiet.”
ON A WARM BOSTON MORNING a few days earlier, Casey is sitting in the public library’s main branch in Copley Square. The bright, airy lobby is home to the live studio for GBH, the city’s public radio affiliate, and hosts Jim Braude and Margery Eagan are talking with Healey for her monthly “Ask the Governor” segment. A couple of dozen retirees, as well as a young guy wearing a Dropkick Murphys St. Patrick’s Day tour shirt, watch her take call-in questions on everything from post-partum healthcare (Lindsay Clancy’s case just ended in a mistrial) to nuclear power, data centers, opioid addiction, and the state’s ties to the Israel-Palestine conflict. She patiently addresses each caller, continually referring back to her commitment to upholding the civil rights of all citizens, no matter their color, creed, or sexual orientation. Toward the end of the segment, Casey joins her to discuss a bill he’s been helping her promote, which would cap resale prices of concert tickets, as well as the recent debacle involving Ed Sheeran, Macklemore, and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft.
On air, his language is significantly less profane than it is onstage, but the message remains just as forceful. “The fact that Ed Sheeran took the knee, no matter what the cause is, and [didn’t stand] with his fellow tour partner, just doesn’t sit right with me,” he tells the audience . “And that’s not how Dropkick Murphys would operate.” He seems confident standing there next to his friend the governor, as well as Eagon and Braude, the latter of whom has become a mentor of sorts as Casey’s public profile has grown. He’s been a guest on their show multiple times, and even guest-hosted on a few instances. After the segment, as we walk across the street to retrieve his car from a hotel valet, he tells me that he hopes to someday start his own radio show, if he can find the time amid the band’s tour schedule. In the meantime, he’s starting a podcast with Michael Fanone , the police officer who was assaulted by rioters on Jan. 6, 2021, who is also a longtime Dropkicks fan. “He was at the very first D.C. show we ever played,” Casey says.
“There’s still Nazis in the punk and skinhead scene? Who gives a fuck if there are. The president is a fucking Nazi.”
Casey is a natural podcast host, if for no other reason than his voice — what Springsteen will later describe to me as “his true Irish tenor.” He has a warm presence, and when he smiles, his eyes shrink behind his cheeks. Though he gets deadly serious many times during our conversations, he’s quick to laugh and seems to delight at meeting fans wherever they might crop up. Before we leave the library, he says hi to the kid in the Dropkicks shirt; when he’s getting the car from the valet, one of the doormen asks for a selfie. “My dad is going to be so excited,” he tells Casey, who grabs his hand and eagerly poses. He’s the city’s unpretentious mascot, a stout divorcé with three grown kids, a passion for union politics and Celtic-tinged punk, and an almost pathological drive to stand up for what’s right.
As soon as Dropkicks showed up in the Nineties, it was as if they had some kind of innate knowledge of how to make a punk band successful. “It almost seemed like they had a grown-up idea of how to do this thing that we were all figuring out as kids,” says James Lynch, who joined them as a guitarist when he was 20, but had been playing in Boston punk bands for years. “When the Dropkicks come on the scene singing about union labor and all this stuff, we’re all singing along with it, with no idea what they’re talking about. It was just something special from the jump.”
Back in 1996, Casey was newly married, working construction, and tending bar, putting himself through the local UMass, where he was taking classes to be a special ed teacher. “I didn’t know if I’d ever get there,” he says, as we drive through Boston in his giant black SUV, making our way from the ritzy Back Bay to South Boston, the once-working-class part of town that’s since been overtaken by glass condos and rising rents. “I was special ed in high school — not because I had a learning disability. I was an alcoholic. I was a chronic truant, and in an effort to keep me caught up and engaged, they put me in a special ed room.” These days, he notes, that would never fly, “but back then they didn’t know what to do with me. I got out of high school by the skin of my teeth.”
At 26, he was five years sober, and channeling some of that new free time into booking all-ages matinees at the Rathskeller (better known as the Rat), a local institution known for launching generations of Boston bands; putting out singles and splits on his label, Flat Records; and publishing band interviews in its accompanying zine, Flat Magazine.
Around that time, a fellow bartender who was enrolled at the prestigious Berklee College of Music offered Casey a proposition. “You’re always talking about starting a band,” Casey recalls him saying. “My band has a show in three weeks, I dare you to open for us.” So he took his coworker up on it. “Just out of pride and wanting to win the bet.”
Casey called up another friend, Bill Close, guitarist for the 1980s Cape Cod hardcore band the Freeze, who offered to play drums and teach Casey to play bass. “We had three weeks to come up with a name, so we did the first show under the moniker of the Snots,” Casey says. “Needless to say, had we stuck with that, I probably wouldn’t have just been on public radio with the governor.” But he wasn’t sure of his chops as a singer, so he recruited Mike McColgan, a Gulf War vet and fellow Boston punk, for vocals.
By their second gig, the band was calling themselves Dropkick Murphys. By the third — opening for a Freeze reunion show — they were playing for a whole room of strangers. Soon, they had an “undeniable buzz,” Casey says, selling 200 copies of their six-song EP, Boys on the Docks , at each show. The Mighty Mighty Bosstones tapped them for tour, and by the middle of 1997, Rancid’s Tim Armstrong had asked them to record an album for his new Epitaph subsidiary. All four members quit their jobs to focus on the band full-time. “I don’t know that everyone thought it was going to be a career, by any means,” Casey says. “We just thought, ‘We’re going to quit our jobs at the same time, and all go back to our jobs at the same time.’”
It didn’t hurt that the Boston punk scene was thriving. “The Rat at the time — and Boston in general — the mid-Nineties punk scene here was just unbelievable,” Casey says, reeling off local bands they came up with: the Unseen, Showcase Showdown, the Ducky Boys, the Trouble. “We were all drawing more than what you would have thought.” It helped on the road, too: Bands that visited Boston would be virtually guaranteed a packed house, so when Boston bands went to their towns, those bands went out of their way to make sure folks came out.
“At the time, if you started a band and you were from Boston, you had someone waiting to put out your record,” says Lynch. “I remember being at the Rat one time, at a Ducky Boys show, and [singer] Mark [Lind] was like, ‘People were always talking about what it was like to be at CBGBs in the Seventies. Someday, people are going to be talking about the Nineties at the Rat.’ It was like some big, never-ending summer camp.” (Last year, for their 30th anniversary, Dropkicks got a handful of the old bands to reunite, filling out the bills for three nights at the MGM Music Hall at Fenway. “People just fucking loved it,” Casey says.)
Being in Dropkicks, though, was not a vacation. Used to working labor jobs, Casey wanted this new gig to feel real, meaning practice would often start at 7 a.m. “It’s this work ethic thing,” he says. “It’s like, how can I have a job if I’m not doing my job?” The band members could handle it, but the property manager who lived above their first rehearsal spot was less enthusiastic. “He’d get up: ‘What the fuck are you doing?’ ‘We practice in the morning because it makes us feel responsible.’ He’s like, ‘No no, that’s why you get in a band, so you don’t have to do that.’ And I’m like, that’s not how we think of being in a band.”
When they weren’t rehearsing, they’d be writing, or helping out in the community, like going to play an acoustic set at a hospital. They made their own merch, pressed their own records, did their own promo. “Being in a band can sometimes feel self-indulgent,” Casey says. But keeping things DIY made it feel like a career.
Though Casey is the only founding member still in Dropkicks — the others left, he says, largely because they weren’t up for the intense touring schedule — the core group has been pretty steady for the past 20 years. Drummer Matt Kelly joined in 1997, Lynch came on in 2000, guitarist Tim Brennan came on in 2002, and multi-instrumentalist Jeff DaRosa came on in 2007. Rounding out their onstage ensemble are touring bassist Kevin Rheault, who’s been with the band since 2017, and touring bagpiper Campbell Webster, who joined in 2022. From the get-go, bagpipers proved the hardest musicians to keep. “Sometimes the bagpipe [player] that we had might have been in a pipe band at home and had a civil service job,” Casey says. “Sometimes they were just not built to last in a band with seven people.”
But the blend of Celtic music and punk was a surefire hit. Even before they brought in banjos and bagpipes, the musical phrasing hinted at their influences, and fans loved it. Not surprisingly, all the band members cite the Pogues as an influence; singer Shane MacGowan even guested on the 2001 track “Good Rats,” about a group of rodents getting drunk at a brewery off-hours. (In November, their cover of the Pogues’ “Body of an American” will appear on the compilation 20th Century Paddy – The Songs of Shane MacGowan. ) From the start, blending the two felt natural to Casey: “Celtic music was in my fucking genes, and punk rock was my teenage music of choice.” When he first heard the Pogues, he felt like the band “was genetically engineered for me,” he says. Lynch felt similarly about Dropkicks. “My grandfather played Irish music; my dad played punk rock,” the guitarist tells me. “It’s like I was grown in a petri dish to be in this band.”
“I DON’T KNOW WHETHER it’s pride, or some kind of neurological disorder, but I want to push a rock up the hill and get it there,” Casey tells me, digging into a cardboard tray of fried clam bellies, sipping a Diet Coke from a waxed paper cup. We’ve made our way to Castle Island, where we sit on a bench, looking over a serene Boston Harbor, where a handful of pissed-off Bostonians once dumped a boatload of tea to protest British taxation. Now a state park, the first fort on this peninsula was established in the 1630s. It functioned as a strategic outpost through World War II, defending the city and the nation from Axis attacks. Casey, however, is talking about the enemy within.
For the past decade or so, Casey has been a hard voice against Trump, ever since “he fucking came down the escalator.” The band had always been outspoken in a 1990s punk sort of way, contributing the song “We’ve Got the Power” to the 2004 Fat Wreck Chords comp Rock Against Bush, Vol. 2 , covering the union classic “Which Side Are You On?” on their 2001 album, Sing Loud, Sing Proud! , beating up any Nazi that dared to come into their pit. But it wasn’t until the modern far-right started coalescing, and Trump used that anti-immigrant, anti-worker momentum to launch his campaign, that Casey’s political rhetoric turned more public.
Dropkicks’ first moment of this type of virality came earlier in 2015, when then-Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, who’d run for office on his intent to weaken collective bargaining, used “I’m Shipping Up to Boston” as his walkout song for a speech at the Iowa Freedom Summit. Casey was enraged. “Using a Dropkick Murphys song as an intro is like a white supremacist coming out to gangsta rap,” he wrote on Facebook. But it was his tweet that really got people talking. “Please stop using our music in any way,” he wrote, tagging the governor. “We literally hate you!!! Love, Dropkick Murphys.”
Casey was surprised by how much attention it brought them. “It just goes to show how many of those fucking Republican politicians are so out of touch,” he says, “using the song by someone who does, in fact, literally hate you.”
A few years later, in Clearwater, Florida, they had another moment when Casey called out an audience member in the front row who was wearing a MAGA shirt and hat. “In the name of dialogue and discourse — and I appreciate you being here — would you agree to a friendly wager?” Casey asked from the stage. The man agreed. Casey pulled out a Dropkicks T-shirt, and he noted to the crowd that the band only sells merch made by American workers.
“If you lose the bet, [you] switch shirts. If you win the bet, I give you $100 and the shirt,” he said. “You can’t lose!” The audience member took the bet. Their tour manager checked the tag on the MAGA shirt and shouted up to the stage. “It’s made in Nicaragua!” Casey announced, before giving the guy the band tee and thanking him for being a good sport.
“Sometimes I feel like being in the band keeps you young. Other times, it’ll make you feel old if you’re not ready.”
“A lot of people are like, ‘Why are you wasting your breath talking to MAGA?’ I usually don’t, but it was nice to feel like, fuck. I made a point,” he says now. Even better, it gave him a glimmer of hope. “The reaction online shows that deep down in their hearts, the country wants to believe that some element of us can come back together again.”
Long before phrases like “replacement theory” made their way into mainstream politics, Dropkicks had plenty of experience dealing with people on the far right. Nazi skinheads had been a thing since Britain’s National Front party started recruiting punks with shaved heads in the 1970s. Two decades later, the tradition was still strong in the U.S. Though they weren’t really present in Boston proper — the local anti-Nazi skinhead group FSU , short for Friends Stand United (or Fuck Shit Up, depending on who you ask), would beat up anyone suspected of harboring far-right views, or really “anyone they didn’t know,” Casey jokes — they were definitely an issue on tour. “Our shows would oftentimes be the breeding ground for Nazis coming looking for S.H.A.R.P.s,” or Skin Heads Against Racial Prejudice, Casey says, particularly in places like Colorado and Florida.
He remembers a tour where they had the “bright idea” to bring street hockey sticks and nets on tour. “We were still young and thought, well, in the venues we can have street hockey games after sound check,” he says. The games were largely a punt, but the gear ended up coming in handy for other reasons. One night after a show, as they waited to load into their bus, he says, Nazis started circling the venue. The band sent a roadie out as a decoy, and the Nazis stopped the car, ready to give him a beatdown. “Little did they know, all of us — our crew, whoever we had on tour — were around the other side with hockey sticks,” Casey remembers. “We came running around and smashed all their windows out, and may or may not have hit a few people.”
While on tour with the British Oi! band the Business in 1998, they were supposed to play a show in Florida, but had to cancel after McColgan quit the band. The Business canceled too, but for another reason: They found out the day before that the venue they were set to play was a white power clubhouse. “So all the bands they had playing are all white power bands,” Casey says. “The fans start showing up for Dropkicks and the Business, and they don’t even tell them we’re not playing. They take the money, [the fans] all come in, and it’s all these Nazi bands playing. This kid went back and said, ‘It’s not what I paid for, give me my money back.’” An argument broke out, and the 25-year-old fan was beaten nearly to death, his throat slashed with a broken beer bottle. “What happened wasn’t even fair,” one witness told the Tampa Tribune . “There was nothing I could do. They were all over this guy.”
Casey wasn’t surprised when he saw these fascist elements start to encroach on nonpunk spaces more recently. In 2022, members of the now-defunct neo-Nazi group NSC 131 rolled up to the St. Patrick’s Day Parade with white masks and a banner reading “Keep Boston Irish”; the Nazis later did “a little highlight reel,” as Casey calls it, setting images from the parade to Dropkicks’ song “The Boys Are Back.” “Stop using our song for your little dress up party video. We will SMASH you,” Casey tweeted, before serving the group with a cease and desist. He then sent them an invitation of sorts: “I’ll be down M street park walking my dogs if [y’all] are looking to discuss,” he wrote, referring to a nearby public park, and gave them a date and time.
“I didn’t want to, in a public forum, say I’ll be down there with a bunch of guys, because then the cops would come,” he tells me. “I had probably 200 guys down there. Friends of mine. The ironworkers sent 40 guys down. Of course, [NSC] never showed up. All these groups, doing their little marches. They’re just fuckin’ nerds. Who thinks khakis and a blue shirt is a threatening outfit?”
He takes a bite of a french fry. “For the most part, there are no Nazis in the scene,” Casey says. “Nowadays, no one needs to try to convince some young kids with shaved heads to be their foot soldiers. It’s the college campuses now, these nerds that are the young Republicans or whatever — you see their group text leak. They’re the fucking white power people now.” They don’t have the same intimidating look, maybe, “but they’re sure scary at what they’re doing politically.” He sees a fascist takeover that has happened “from the ground up,
